name: Kazakhstan
summary: The world’s largest landlocked country, independent since the Soviet Union broke up in 1991, rich in oil, gas and uranium.

knownFor.label: Baikonur Cosmodrome
knownFor.note: Launch site of Sputnik and Gagarin, leased to Russia.

knownFor.label: Astana
knownFor.note: A new capital with futuristic buildings.

knownFor.label: Beshbarmak
knownFor.note: Boiled meat with noodles, the national dish.

location.value: Central Asia, from the Caspian Sea to the Altai; about 2.7 million km².

terrain.value: Steppe, semi-desert and mountains in the south-east.

climate.value: Very continental, with hot summers, harsh cold winters and little rain across the steppe and desert.

resources.value: Oil, gas, uranium (largest producer), coal, wheat.

disasters.value: Soviet nuclear bomb tests at the Semipalatinsk test site, founded in 1947.

population.value: About 19–20 million people in the early 2020s, spread thinly over a huge area.

urbanisation.value: Astana is the capital; Almaty, the capital until 1997, is the largest city.

disease.value: Soviet nuclear tests near Semipalatinsk (1949–89) harmed the health of nearby people.

migration.value: About a million Germans and many Russians lived there before 1991; the population fell from 16.4 to 14.8 million by 2001, mostly as Russians emigrated.

economicBase.value: Oil, gas, uranium and metal mining, plus wheat farming and livestock.

tradeRoutes.value: Pipelines to China and Russia; the Caspian Pipeline.

wealth.value: An upper-middle-income country, mainly because of oil and mineral wealth.

moneyAndTax.value: The tenge, introduced in 1993 after leaving the Soviet rouble.

inequality.value: Gaps between oil-rich elites and others.

governmentType.value: A presidential republic; in practice, power has long been held by the presidency.

keyRulers.value: Kazakhstan has had a small number of presidents since 1990; individual leaders are not named here.

succession.value: Elections have been tightly managed, and the first president ruled from 1991 until 2019.

institutions.value: A strong presidency, a two-chamber parliament (Mazhilis and Senate) and a constitutional court, with the constitution amended in 2022.

stability.value: Large protests after a sharp rise in fuel prices (January 2022).

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry among elite groups over wealth and power, which erupted in the unrest of January 2022.

armyAndTech.value: A small army, with membership of the Russian-led CSTO military alliance.

majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Kazakhstan; Britannica: Independent Kazakhstan (checked 15 Nov 2026) (no interstate war is described; the page covers domestic unrest, including 17 deaths in Zhanaozen in December 2011 and the January 2022 protests, when CSTO forces were deployed)

territoryChange.value: The borders were inherited from the Soviet Union and settled by treaties with Russia and China.

alliancesRivals.value: A “multi-vector” foreign policy, seeking equal relations with Russia, China and the West.

inventions.value: The Baikonur Cosmodrome, used for the first human spaceflight in 1961, lies in Kazakhstan and is leased to Russia.

scienceEducation.value: Literacy is almost universal, a legacy of Soviet schooling.

openness.value: Open to foreign investment, though less open politically.

communicationTransport.value: Railways and roads now link China with Europe across Kazakhstan; the capital moved from Almaty to Astana in 1997.

religion.value: Islam is the largest religion, followed by Eastern Orthodox Christianity.

languageWriting.value: Kazakh and Russian; Kazakh moving to the Latin alphabet.

artsArchitecture.value: Modern architecture in Astana; dombra music.

socialStructure.value: Ethnically diverse: Kazakhs are the majority, with Russians and many others.

sharedIdentity.value: Kazakh language and culture were revived after 1991, while a civic “Kazakhstani” identity is promoted.

dailyLife.value: Apartments in cities; meat and dairy dishes.

neighbours.value: Russia, China, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan, with a coast on the Caspian Sea.

ideasReligions.value: A policy of ethnic and religious harmony; most people are Sunni Muslim or Orthodox Christian.

colonisation.value: Part of the Russian Empire and USSR before 1991.

riseSignals.value: Proclaimed independence on 16 December 1991, the last Soviet republic to do so.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Kazakhstan (checked 8 Nov 2026); Britannica: Independent Kazakhstan (checked 15 Nov 2026) (sovereignty was declared on 25 October 1990 and full independence on 16 December 1991; the page does not say it was the last Soviet republic to leave)

peakPeriod.value: The oil boom of the 2000s, when the economy grew rapidly.

declineSignals.value: Heavy dependence on oil and gas prices makes the economy vulnerable.

outcome.value: Kazakhstan continues as an independent republic.
